title: the Sri Sukta
hook: a fruit with a shell you need a hammer for, and a tree the hymn says was born from the goddess's discipline

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta turned to her directly: I take refuge, I choose you. Today, a tree.

The bilva fruit does not look generous. It's round and greenish-gold, with a shell so hard that people crack it against a stone step or with the back of a cleaver. Inside is a sticky, fragrant pulp that some families stir into a cool summer drink. It's the same tree whose leaves this path saw offered to Shiva. You might expect a softer fruit for a goddess of abundance, a mango, maybe. But when the Sri Sukta names her tree, it names this one. And it says where the tree came from.
screen: `A SHELL YOU NEED A HAMMER FOR.` → `FRAGRANT PULP INSIDE.` → `HER TREE IS THE BILVA.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. O you who are the color of the sun, from your tapas the lord of the forest was born: your tree, the bilva. May its fruits, by tapas, drive away the misfortunes within and without. Start with tapas. It means heat, and then the heat of discipline: effort, austerity, the steady inner fire of someone who keeps at a hard practice. In the old stories, it's the fire sages keep burning in the forest. And here's the surprise: the hymn gives tapas to Sri. The goddess of fortune, gold and ease is the one whose discipline makes the tree grow. In this line, abundance isn't the opposite of effort. It comes out of it. Then the tree. Lord of the forest is an old way of saying a great tree. Its fruits have a job, to push away misfortune, and they do it by tapas too: the heat that grew the tree works through what it bears. Now, misfortunes within and without. The outer ones are easy to list: a failed harvest, an empty purse, a roof that leaks. The inner ones are harder to name. Some readers hear confusion there, illusion, the habits of mind that block a person from within. Others hear the plain sense, trouble inside the house as well as outside it. Either way, fortune isn't only something out there. And it chose a fruit you can't open without effort. Some readers find that fitting: the good thing is inside, and getting to it takes a little heat.
screen: `THE COLOR OF THE SUN.` · `TAPAS, THE HEAT OF DISCIPLINE.` · `HER TREE, THE BILVA.` · `MISFORTUNE WITHIN AND WITHOUT.` · then, large: `ABUNDANCE GROWN FROM EFFORT.`

segments.voice: Choose to stay still, really still, for the whole sit, even when something itches or the mind wants to wander: that's tapas at its smallest, staying a little longer than is comfortable. When the mind wanders, bring it back; the bringing back is the practice. If you pray, you can offer the effort to the goddess, or to God; if you don't, let the stillness be its own offering.
The Sri Sukta. A hymn that says the bilva tree was born from the goddess's own tapas, and asks its fruit to drive away misfortune within and without.
Your line: the Sri Sukta. In this line, abundance grows out of effort. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The bilva tree is treated as sacred in Hindu worship, where its leaves are offered, and this verse is recited as part of the Sri Sukta in Lakshmi worship.

chat.says: Why would the goddess of fortune's tree be the hard-shelled bilva?
options: The hymn says it grew from her own tapas, her discipline: abundance comes out of effort.
Because she wanted a fruit nobody could steal, so her wealth would stay locked inside.
Because the bilva is the only tree that grows beside her lotus pond in the stories.
chat.meaning: In the Sri Sukta the bilva is born from Sri's own tapas, the heat of discipline, and its fruit drives away misfortune within and without.

sources.ref: Sri Sukta, verse 6 (Rig Veda khila, as commonly recited)

notes: Verse 6 paraphrased: ādityavarṇe tapaso 'dhijāto vanaspatis tava vṛkṣo 'tha bilvaḥ / tasya phalāni tapasā nudantu māyāntarāyāś ca bāhyā alakṣmīḥ. māyāntarāyāḥ is read variously ('illusions and inner obstacles', 'misfortunes within'); the script gives two readings without ranking. Confirm.
'In the old stories, it's the fire sages keep burning in the forest' refers to tapas in earlier Hindu path lessons; confirm it was taught.
Bilva (Aegle marmelos, bael): hard shell and pulp used in a summer drink are everyday descriptions; confirm. howItsDone says bilva leaves are offered in worship (common in Shiva worship).
'Some readers find that fitting' (the hard shell as image of effort) is an interpretive image; confirm or cut.
